{{Short description|Repeatable pattern of differences between prime numbers}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Prime ''k''-tuple}}
In [[number theory]], a '''prime {{mvar|k}}-tuple''' is a finite collection of values representing a repeatable pattern of differences between [[prime numbers]].  For a {{mvar|k}}-[[tuple]] {{math|(''a'', ''b'', …)}}, the positions where the {{mvar|k}}-tuple matches a pattern in the prime numbers are given by the set of [[integers]] {{mvar|n}} for which all of the values {{math|(''n'' + ''a'', ''n'' + ''b'', …)}} are prime. Typically the first value in the {{mvar|k}}-tuple is 0 and the rest are distinct positive [[even numbers]].<ref>Chris Caldwell, [https://t5k.org/glossary/page.php?sort=ktuple "The Prime Glossary: ''k''-tuple"] at [[The Prime Pages]].</ref>

==Named patterns==
Several of the shortest ''k''-tuples are known by other common names:

|-
| (0, 4, 6, 10, 12, 16) || [[Prime quadruplet#Prime sextuplets|prime sextuplets]]
|}

[[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|OEIS]] [[oeis:A257124|sequence A257124]] covers 7-tuples (''prime septuplets'') and contains an overview of related sequences, e.g. the three sequences corresponding to the three [[#Admissibility|admissible]] 8-tuples (''prime octuplets''), and the union of all 8-tuples. The first term in these sequences corresponds to the first prime in the smallest [[#Prime constellations|prime constellation]] shown below.

==Admissibility==
In order for a {{mvar|k}}-tuple to have infinitely many positions at which all of its values are prime, there cannot exist a prime {{mvar|p}} such that the tuple includes every different possible value [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] {{mvar|p}}. If such a prime {{mvar|p}} existed, then no matter which value of {{mvar|n}} was chosen, one of the values formed by adding {{mvar|n}} to the tuple would be divisible by {{mvar|p}}, so the only possible placements would have to include {{mvar|p}} itself, and there are at most {{mvar|k}} of those.  For example, the numbers in a {{mvar|k}}-tuple cannot take on all three values 0, 1, and 2 modulo 3; otherwise the resulting numbers would always include a multiple of 3 and therefore could not all be prime unless one of the numbers is 3 itself.

A {{mvar|k}}-tuple that includes every possible residue modulo {{mvar|p}} is said to be '''inadmissible modulo {{mvar|p}}'''.  It should be obvious that this is only possible when {{math|''k'' &geq; ''p''}}.  A tuple which is not inadmissible modulo {{mvar|p}} is called '''admissible'''.

It is [[conjectured]] that every admissible {{mvar|k}}-tuple matches infinitely many positions in the sequence of prime numbers. However, there is no tuple for which this has been [[mathematical proof|proven]] except the trivial 1-tuple (0). In that case, the conjecture is equivalent to the statement that there are [[Euclid's theorem|infinitely many primes]]. Nevertheless, [[Yitang Zhang]] proved in 2013 that there exists at least one 2-tuple which matches infinitely many positions; subsequent work showed that such a 2-tuple exists with values differing by 246 or less that matches infinitely many positions.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Polymath | first = D. H. J. | author-link = Polymath Project
 | article-number = 12
 | doi = 10.1186/s40687-014-0012-7
 | journal = Research in the Mathematical Sciences
 | mr = 3373710
 | title = Variants of the Selberg sieve, and bounded intervals containing many primes
 | volume = 1
 | year = 2014| doi-access = free | arxiv = 1407.4897
 }}</ref>

===Positions matched by inadmissible patterns===
Although {{nowrap|(0, 2, 4)}} is inadmissible modulo 3, it does produce a single set of primes: {{nowrap|(3, 5, 7)}}.

Because 3 is the first odd prime, a non-trivial ({{math|''k'' &geq; 1}}) {{mvar|k}}-tuple matching the prime 3 can only match in one position.  If the tuple begins {{nowrap|(0, 1, ...)}} (i.e. is inadmissible modulo 2) then it can only match {{nowrap|(2, 3, ...);}} if the tuple contains only even numbers, it can only match {{nowrap|(3, ...).}}

Inadmissible {{mvar|k}}-tuples can have more than one all-prime solution if they are admissible modulo 2 and 3, and inadmissible modulo {{math|''p'' &geq; 5}}.  This of course implies that there must be at least five numbers in the tuple.  The shortest inadmissible tuple with more than one solution is the 5-tuple {{nowrap|(0, 2, 8, 14, 26)}}, which has two solutions: {{nowrap|(3, 5, 11, 17, 29)}} and {{nowrap|(5, 7, 13, 19, 31)}}, where all values modulo 5 are included in both cases.  Examples with three or more solutions also exist.<ref>{{cite web |title=How many distinct translates of a (non-admissible) set {{mvar|H}} can consist entirely of primes? |first=Ravi |last=Fernando |date=7 March 2015 |website=Mathematics StackExchange |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/413275/how-many-distinct-translates-of-a-non-admissible-set-mathcalh-can-consist/1180160#1180160}}{{user-generated source|date=January 2026}}</ref>

==Prime constellations==
The '''diameter''' of a {{mvar|k}}-tuple is the difference of its largest and smallest elements. An admissible prime {{mvar|k}}-tuple with the smallest possible diameter {{mvar|d}} (among all admissible {{mvar|k}}-tuples) is a '''prime constellation'''. For all {{math|''n'' ≥ ''k''}} this will always produce consecutive primes.<ref>{{MathWorld|urlname=PrimeConstellation|title=Prime Constellation}}</ref> (Recall that all {{mvar|n}} are integers for which the values {{math|(''n'' + ''a'', ''n'' + ''b'', …)}} are prime.)

This means that, for large {{mvar|n}}:

:<math>p_{n+k-1} - p_n \geq d</math>

where {{mvar|p{{sub|n}}}} is the {{mvar|n}}th prime number.

The first few prime constellations are:

The diameter {{mvar|d}} as a function of {{mvar|k}} is [[oeis:A008407|sequence A008407]] in the [[OEIS]].

A prime constellation is sometimes referred to as a '''prime {{mvar|k}}-tuplet''', but some authors reserve that term for instances that are not part of longer {{mvar|k}}-tuplets.

The [[first Hardy–Littlewood conjecture]] predicts that the asymptotic frequency of any prime constellation can be calculated.  While the conjecture is unproven it is considered likely to be true. If that is the case, it implies that the [[second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture]], in contrast, is false.

==Prime arithmetic progressions==
{{Main|Primes in arithmetic progression}}
A prime {{mvar|k}}-tuple of the form {{math|(0, ''n'', 2''n'', 3''n'', …, (''k'' − 1)''n'')}} is said to be a '''prime arithmetic progression'''.  In order for such a {{mvar|k}}-tuple to meet the admissibility test, {{mvar|n}} must be a multiple of the [[primorial]] of {{mvar|k}}.<ref>{{MathWorld|urlname=PrimeArithmeticProgression|title=Prime Arithmetic Progression}}</ref>

==Skewes numbers==
The [[Skewes's number#Equivalent for prime k-tuples|Skewes numbers for prime ''k''-tuples]] are an extension of the definition of [[Skewes's number]] to prime ''k''-tuples based on the [[first Hardy–Littlewood conjecture]] ({{harvtxt|Tóth|2019}}). Let <math>P = (p,\ p+i_1,\ p+i_2,\ \dots\ ,\ p+i_k)</math> denote a prime {{mvar|k}}-tuple, <math>\pi_P(x)</math> the number of primes {{mvar|p}} below {{mvar|x}} such that <math>p,\ p+i_1,\ p+i_2,\ \dots\ ,\ p+i_k</math> are all prime, let <math display="inline">\operatorname{li}_P(x) = \int_2^x \frac{dt}{(\ln t)^{k + 1}}</math> and let <math>C_P</math> denote its Hardy–Littlewood constant (see [[first Hardy–Littlewood conjecture]]). Then the first prime {{mvar|p}} that violates the Hardy–Littlewood inequality for the {{mvar|k}}-tuple {{mvar|P}}, i.e., such that
: <math>\pi_P(p) > C_P \operatorname{li}_P(p), </math>
(if such a prime exists) is the ''Skewes number for {{mvar|P}}''.
